'''Robert H. Wurtz''' is an American [[neuroscientist]] working as a [[NIH]] Distinguished Scientist and Chief of the Section on Visuomotor Integration at the [[National Eye Institute]]. He is a member of the [[US National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. He is recognized for developing methods for studying the [[visual system]] in "awake-behaving" primates (as opposed to those under anesthesia), a technique now widely used for the study of higher brain functions. He pioneered the study of the [[neuronal]] basis of vision and its relation with [[cognitive]] functions.<ref>{{cite web|title= Robert Wurtz |year=2012 | url= http://www.crsltd.com/guest-talks/crs-guest-lecturers/robert-wurtz/ |work= www.crsltd.com|publisher=Cambridge Research Systems Ltd. |access-date= 3 September 2013}}</ref>

==Early life and education==

Robert Wurtz was born in [[Saint Louis, Missouri]] and grew up in the nearby suburb of Webster Groves. He was the only child of Robert Henry Wurtz. His father was a factory superintendent for the Mavrakos Candy Company and his mother, Alice Edith (Popplewell), was a [[bookkeeper]] at the same company.<ref name=SfN/>

He had wanted to attend a [[Liberal arts colleges in the United States|liberal arts college]], but his father persuaded him to apply to [[Oberlin College]], from which he graduated in 1958, with a major in chemistry.<ref name=SfN>{{Citation|title=The History of Neuroscience in Autobiography Volume 7 | url=https://www.sfn.org/-/media/SfN/Documents/TheHistoryofNeuroscience/Volume-7/c16.pdf|publisher=Society for Neuroscience| ISBN=0-19-539613-8}}</ref>

Wurtz developed an interest in experimental psychology and physiology of the [[nervous system]], and subsequently studied psychology under [[James Olds]] at [[University of Michigan]].<ref name=":0" /> He submitted his PhD thesis in 1962, despite that Olds was hesitant about the title, ''Self-Stimulation and Escape in Response to Stimulation of the Rat Amygdala''. He continued post-doctoral research in the physiology department of [[Washington University in St. Louis]].<ref>{{cite web| author=Robert H. Wurtz |title=Robert H. Wurtz (autobiography) | url= http://www.sfn.org/~/media/SfN/Documents/TheHistoryofNeuroscience/Volume%207/c16.ashx |work= www.sfn.org |publisher=Society for Neuroscience |access-date= 3 September 2013}}</ref>

==Professional career==

In 1966, Wurtz joined the Laboratory of Neurobiology, [[National Institute of Mental Health]], in [[Bethesda, Maryland]]. He began studies on the visual system of awake in monkeys and made groundbreaking works on [[neurobiology]] of vision and eye movements. During this time he spent a year (1975-1976) as a visiting scientist at the Physiological Laboratory at [[Cambridge University]] in England. He became the founding Chief of the Laboratory of Sensorimotor Research, National Eye Institute in 1978. In 2002, he stepped down as chief of the laboratory, but has remained as a senior investigator.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title= 2010 Neuroscience Prize: Robert H. Wurtz|year= 2010| url= http://gruber.yale.edu/neuroscience/robert-h-wurtz |work= gruber.yale.edu |publisher= The Gruber Foundation|access-date= 3 September 2013}}</ref>

His 1969 publications became classic papers on this technique of studying the physiology of the visual system,<ref>{{cite journal |author= Wurtz RH |title= Visual receptive fields of striate cortex neurons in awake monkeys |journal=J Neurophysiol  |volume= 32|issue=5 | pages= 727–742 |year= 1969 |pmid=4980023 |doi= 10.1152/jn.1969.32.5.727}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author= Wurtz RH |title= Response of striate cortex neurons to stimuli during rapid eye movements in the monkey |journal= J Neurophysiol |volume=32 |issue= 6 | pages= 975–986 |year= 1969 |pmid=4981518 |doi= 10.1152/jn.1969.32.6.975}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author= Wurtz RH |title= Comparison of effects of eye movements and stimulus movements on striate cortex neurons of the monkey |journal= J Neurophysiol |volume= 32|issue= 6 | pages= 987–994 |year= 1969 |pmid= 4981519|doi= 10.1152/jn.1969.32.6.987}}</ref> and now used by [[Cognitive scientist|cognitive neuroscientists]] around the world.

==Personal life==

Robert Wurtz married Sally Smith, a fellow student at Oberlin, c. 1955. They have a son William and a daughter Erica.<ref name=SfN/>

==Award and recognition==

*[[W. Alden Spencer Award]], Columbia University (1987)
*Elected member of the National Academy of Sciences (1988)
*Elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1990)
*President, [[Society for Neuroscience]] (1991)
*1991 [[Golden Brain Award]] from [[Minerva Foundation]]<ref>{{cite web|title= 1991: Wurtz|date= 29 November 1991|url= http://www.minervaberkeley.org/golden-brain/1991-wurtz|work= www.minervaberkeley.org|access-date= 3 September 2013|archive-date= 4 May 2017|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170504210814/http://www.minervaberkeley.org/golden-brain/1991-wurtz/|url-status= dead}}</ref>
*[[Karl Spencer Lashley Award]], [[American Philosophical Society]] (1995)
*Friedenwald Award, Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology (1996)
*Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award, [[American Psychological Association]] (1997)
*Institute of Medicine of the National Academy of Sciences (1997)
*[[Dan David Prize]] for the Future Time Dimension: “Brain Sciences” (2004)
*[[Ralph W. Gerard Prize in Neuroscience]], Society for Neuroscience (2006)
*Honorary Doctor of Science, Oberlin College (2009)
*Grass Lecture, Society for Neuroscience (2009)
*[[Gruber Prize in Neuroscience]] (2010)
